shippingNews.postTitle: Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway Tonnage Up 3.5 Percent Through End of September

stories.body: Saltwater tanker transits the St. Lawrence Seaway. [Photo SLSMC] WELLAND CANAL – Nearly 25 million tonnes of cargo passed through the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway System by the end of September, up 3.5 per cent compared to the same time last year. It’s the second positive increase of the 2026 season, which began with March openings of the Welland Canal and Montreal-Lake Ontario sections of the 3,700-kilometre-long waterway. todayInHistory.title: Sam Laud
todayInHistory.text: Sam Laud Bay Shipbuilding Corp. of Sturgeon Bay, WI, laid the keel for their hull # 712 on Jan. 4, 1974 to be built as a smaller-sized Great Lakes self-unloading bulk cargo carrier. The new vessel was launched on Nov. 19, 1974 for Buffalo's American Steamship Co. (ASC), a subsidiary of GATX Corp., Chicago, IL. Completed in 1975, the self-unloader was christened Sam Laud by Mrs. Edna Laud on behalf of her husband at a christening ceremony held April 15, 1975. Mr. Laud was the former president (1945) and chairman of the board (1956) of GATX Corp., having started with the company in 1916 as shop painter and riveter. Mr. Laud died August 1, 1963. GATX Corp. had acquired ASC in July of 1973. Mrs. Laud was accompanied by Mr. Frederick G. Jaicks, chairman and CEO of Inland Steel Co., Chicago, IL, who gave the address at the christening ceremonies. One of a new generation of self-unloaders for the ASC fleet, the Sam Laud was built at an approximate cost of $13.3 million and was the fourth of 10 self-unloaders launched for the fleet under Chapter XI of the Merchant Marine Act of 1970. Under this act, the U.S. government-guaranteed financing and tax deferred benefits for fleet modernizing. The other ASC self-unloaders built under this program were the Roger M. Kyes (now Adam E. Cornelius, 1973), Charles E. Wilson (now John J. Boland, 1973), H. Lee White (1974), St. Clair (1976), Belle River (now Walter J. marineWeather.synopsis: A 30.5 inch high pressure over New England is extending a 30.2 inch ridge over Lake Superior this morning. By this afternoon, a 29.2 inch low over northern Manitoba drags a 30.1 inch trough over the west half of Lake Superior. The trough remains over the lake until tonight. High pressure of 30.6 inches over the Canadian Prairies on Sunday pushes ridging of 30.4 inches over the Upper Great Lakes. The high pressure moves over northern Ontario at 30.5 inches Monday into Tuesday. A weak 30.0 inch low lifts north over Minnesota on Tuesday. Then, a 29.8 inch low quickly follows a similar northeast track over the Dakotas/northwestern Minnesota Tuesday night into Wednesday while the high moves to New England. The low then tracks northeast over northern Ontario on Wednesday.

Low pressure near 29.2 inches will progress toward the Hudson Bay this evening. Progression of the low will maintain generally southerly flow across the waters, with gusts between 25-30 knots possible over the northern half of the lake this afternoon and tonight. Can't rule out an isolated gust approaching gale force during this time frame, with conditions not widespread enough for headlines. Winds will trend southwesterly while steadily weakening ahead of an approaching cold front on Sunday. Currently expecting the front to move south across Lake Michigan Sunday evening and night, bringing a breezy northeast wind shift. Gales are not anticipated during the frontal passage, with any isolated rain showers expected to remain over the far northern part of the lake. Breezy northeast winds will continue through Monday as 30.7 inch high pressure slides into Ontario from the Canadian Great Plains. Winds will trend easterly and eventually south to southwesterly Tuesday into Thursday as the aforementioned high shifts into the northeastern United States. Widespread rain chances return Wednesday into Friday.

High pressure, 30.50 inches, broadens over New England over the weekend, sustaining an extended period of tranquil and mainly dry conditions over the central Greak Lakes into next week. A cold front will move through on Sunday, with a mainly dry passage.

High pressure 30.50 inches over the New England states will shift south along the East Coast through Sunday. A weak cold front will approach the area on Monday. High pressure 30.50 inches will return from the north on Tuesday and Wednesday.

A ridge averaging 30.5 inches affects the lake through Sunday night as the embedded high pressure center drifts generally southward from southern Quebec toward the Mid-Atlantic states. The ridge then exits southeastward as a weak cold front sweeps southeastward across the lake on Monday. Behind the front, another ridge averaging 30.5 inches affects the lake through this Wednesday as the embedded high pressure center wobbles southeastward from near Manitoba to near the Gulf of Maine.
